newsitem.title: BOLIVIA: Peru military attacked as rebels played - hostage.
newsitem.headline: Peru military attacked as rebels played - hostage.

text.p: Bolivian Ambassador to Peru Jorge Gumucio, one of the hostages freed from the Japanese envoy's residence in Lima on Tuesday, said 10 of the rebels were playing soccer in a large reception room when troops stormed in.

"They had turned the room into an indoor football pitch under which were the tunnels full of explosives... The operation began with explosions under the floor where they were playing and immediately afterwards in other tunnels through which the special troops entered," he told Bolivian television.
The diplomat was one of the prized hostages seized by about 20 Marxist rebels of the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) when they stormed the residence during a cocktail party on December 17.

He said that after months in captivity awaiting rescue, the hostages had just a few minutes to prepare when the rescue attack came. But they had better information than the rebels, since some of the Peruvian military officers who were captives knew about the rescue plan, the diplomat said.

"They warned us 10 minutes beforehand so we could not really prepare. We waited for them to come in and it was surgical, though with some cost especially for the special forces," Gumucio told Bolivian TV by telephone.
The envoy said the operation was supposed to last 10-15 minutes but went on for 10 minutes over schedule.

"We got out of the sector where we were but with bullet wounds. Peruvian Foreign Minister Francisco Tudela had two gunshot wounds in one leg and another in the armpit, but he's not in great danger," he said.

The ambassador said that while the rebels were taken by surprise, and all killed in the astonishingly successful operation, his wife Beatriz told him in a flood of tears upon his release that "she had a premonition since Monday that she was going to see me very soon."

Bolivian President Gonzalo Sanchez de Lozada told reporters in the city of Sucre, where he was hosting a summit of Andean Pact presidents, that he had not been consulted on the operation, despite two visits from Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori during the crisis.

But Bolivian Communications Secretary Mauricio Antezana welcomed the outcome. "For the Bolivian government the most important aim was reached, that was to preserve the lives of the hostages and especially of Ambassador Gumucio," he told reporters.
